extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Indian poetics, drama/theatre practitioners, and creative-writing students studying rasa theory
extracted.subtask_description: Explain or apply Bharata's Rasa theory to create or analyze poetry/drama: how rasa is produced (vibhav, anubhav, sancharibhav, sthayibhav, sattvik bhava), how universalization (sadharanikaran) works, and the characteristics of each rasa (including Shanta).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sadharanikaran (universalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sadharanikaran means transforming the particular into the general so that characters lose individual identity and assume qualities of common men, becoming universalized; this universalization helps the spectator realize rasa and become free from prejudices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bhattanayaka (as explained in Abhinavabharati) elucidates sadharanikaran via three types of Shabda-vyapara (functions of words): abhidha-vyapara (conventional meaning), bhavaktva-vyapara (generalization of vibhav, anubhav and sancharibhav), and bhoj/vyapara (state of enjoyment). Summarized points: (1) transform particular into general; (2) whole action is universalized during manifestation of rasa; (3) spectator becomes free from prejudices in universalization; (4) universalization foregrounds realization of poetic pleasure (rasa); (5) in universalization sthayibhav matures into rasa as it correlates with other bhava.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituents for producing rasa (vibhav, anubhav, sancharibhav, sthayibhav, sattvik bhava)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa is produced when components—vibhav (causes/supports: alambana and uddipana), anubhav (manifested responses), sancharibhav (transitory states), and sthayibhav (permanent mood)—correlate; sattvik bhava (psychophysical responses) are also involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or writing, specify alambana-vibhav (supporting causes, e.g., characters), uddipana-vibhav (excitors: setting, objects), appropriate anubhav (expressive manifestations like gestures/tears), sancharibhav (transitory emotions), and expected sattvik responses (perspiration, trembling, choked voice) so the sthayibhav matures into rasa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bharata's eight principal rasas (and the aim of art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bharata defines eight rasa: Sringara (erotic), Hasya (comic), Karuna (compassionate), Rudra (furious), Vira (heroic), Bhayanak (terrifying), Bibhatsa (disgusting) and Adbhuta (awesome). He emphasizes that the aim of art is pleasure and that rasa should not hurt the spectator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Bharata's taxonomy when classifying dramatic content; note that although emotive content differs, all rasas produce aesthetic pleasure by leading the spectator into a general/universal emotional ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sringara Rasa (erotic/love)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sringara arises from the sthayibhav of love; associated with bright, pure, beautiful elements and has alambana vibhav (young noble men and women), uddipana vibhav (seasons, garlands, music, gardens), anubhav (eye-use, felicitous movements, soft speech) and accompanying transitory emotions (laziness, violence, disgust).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict Sringara with gorgeous setting (gardens, moonlight, perfumes), employ anubhav appropriate to union (sambhog) or separation (vipralamba), and be aware of two classical types: sambhog (union) and vipralamba (separation); Dasarupaka added a third (ayoga). Sringara is often treated as 'rasa raja'—the supreme rasa—but claims that all rasas originate from it are contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Karuna Rasa (compassion/pathos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Karuna's central emotion is sorrow (soka) and it proceeds from vibhav such as curse, separation, downfall, loss, death, imprisonment, calamity; it is said to stem from Rudra (furious).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Karuna evokes painful emotions, aesthetic pleasure arises when the sahardya universalizes the sorrow (egoless identification), producing vicarious/transcendental pleasure. Use skilful representation and literary power to transform worldly pain into aesthetic experience; list sancharibhav examples: despondency, despair, pangs of death, worry, illness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudra Rasa (anger/fury)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rudra has anger (krodh) as its permanent emotion; characters include demons, monsters, violent men; arises from vibhav like insult, envy, assault, oppressive acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict Rudra with actions of wrath and fury—roaring, violent movements, reddened eyes; recognize that Rudra's krodh is stationary (anger that does not lead to energetic action) and that sancharibhav include indignation, pride. Rudra is considered one of the fundamental rasas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vira Rasa (heroic/heroism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vira consists in dynamic energy (utsaha) with sthayibhav enthusiasm; vibhav include correct perception, decisiveness, political wisdom, army, eminence, etc.; acted out by firmness, bravery, courage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish Vira from Rudra: Vira's utsaha turns anger into energetic action (Utsaha primary, Krodh secondary). Use gestures like firmness, martial posture, and sancharibhav such as patience and dignity. Vira may include internal and external conflicts and subdivides (dayavira, yudhavira, danvira).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hasya Rasa (comic/laughter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hasya's primary emotion is laughter (hasa); arises from vibhav like comic dress, awkward gesture, telling fantastic tales, deformity (vyanga), or seeing someone wearing ill-fitting clothes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate types of comic laughter (self-laughter vs causing another to laugh). Hasya should not be generated through vulgarity, farce or meanness; intention must be benign (not to harm). Includes satirical forms (upahasita - scornful laugh; apahasita - mockery/satire). Watch for sancharibhav examples: dissimilation, indolence, sleep, jealousy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adbhuta Rasa (wonder/awesome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adbhuta's permanent emotion is wonder/astonishment (vismaya); arises from vibhav such as seeing heavenly beings, magic, temples, flying chariots, jugglers' shows; sattvik manifestations include perspiration, trembling, choking voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict astonishment through external exciters (color, shape, size, distance) and anubhav (dilation of eyes, tears, tremulous voice). Adbhuta often functions across rasas as the element of wonder causing the heart to expand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bhayanak Rasa (fear/terrifying)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bhayanak has fear (bhaya) as its permanent emotion; arises from vibhav such as ghastly noises, supernatural beings, empty houses, dark forests, hearing of imprisonment or murder of relatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fear can be transmitted either at sufficient aesthetic distance (perception of fear) or by empathy (sharing the victim's fear—common in horror fiction). Use appropriate sancharibhav (disappointment, agitation, fatigue) and stage incidents (ghosts, darkness) to intensify Bhayanak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibhatsa Rasa (disgust/repulsiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bibhatsa's sthayibhav is jugupsa (disgust/repulsion); it arises from vibhav like seeing, hearing, smelling, or touching something slimy, ugly or vulgar; anubhav includes physical reactions (vomiting, spitting, body contraction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage repulsive or ugly scenes to elicit the physiological anubhav: sarvanga samahra (contraction of whole body), mukhavikuna (facial contortions), ullekhana (vomiting), udvejana (violent trembling). Bibhatsa is often primary and can give rise to Bhayanak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shanta Rasa (calm/equilibrium)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shanta involves a state of calm or equilibrium (sama) leading to moksha; arises from vibhav such as knowledge of truth, detachment and purity; anubhav includes meditation, devotion, dharana, yama/niyama, and sattvik signs like stambha and horripilation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is debate about Shanta's status (some deny or subsume it), but defenders argue it is an independent rasa that can be expressed externally and thus be a subject of poetry and drama. Distinguish sthayibhav (sama) from momentary nirveda (sancharibhav); Shanta requires portrayal of internal tendencies culminating in external forms (hilarity/amity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience disposition (sahardya) and the role of gunas
rubrics_metrics.description: Rasa experience requires a sahardya (person of poetic sensibility): magnanimous, cleared-minded, free from prior attachments and prejudices. The gunas (sattva, rajas, tamas) color the subtype of a rasa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For rasa to be successfully experienced, the spectator's mind should be predominated by sattva (goodness); rajas and tamas should be subordinated. Each rasa may have three subtypes depending on the guna-source of sthayibhav (e.g., karuna can be sattvik, rajasik, tamasik depending on cause of grief). Authors/teachers should consider audience's capacity to universalize when composing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasa relationships, classifications, and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Bharata indicates cause-effect relationships among rasas (Sringara–Hasya, Rudra–Karuna, Vira–Adbhuta, Bibhatsa–Bhayanak), and groups certain rasas under dramatic types (Tragedy vs Comedy). He also denies the possibility of entirely new rasas beyond the classical eight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or composing, map dominant/subordinate rasas, use relational pairs to produce secondary rasas, and follow Bharata's proscription that new emotions should fit into the established rasas. Example classification offered: Tragedy: Karuna, Rudra, Vira, Bhayanak, Bibhatsa; Comedy: Sringara, Hasya, Vira, Adbhuta.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maturation rule: sthayibhav correlates with other bhava to become rasa
rubrics_metrics.description: A sthayibhav (permanent mood) matures into rasa only when it correlates with other bhava (vibhav, anubhav, sancharibhav) which become innate in human psyche and are universalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of a scene should verify that the permanent mood is adequately supported by excitors, manifested responses and transitory states so that the spectator's experience moves from particular emotion to universalized rasa.
